Countrymen
kŭn'trə-mən
n. pl. (men of one's own nation; in the New Testament, chiefly those from whom persecution came)
English country, from Latin contrata, the land lying opposite, with men. The Greek genos in Paul's list means race or kindred; sumphuletes in Thessalonians means a fellow tribesman.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Both uses of the word in the Authorized Version stand in a list of sufferings. Paul's catalogue of perils: “In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren” (2Co 11:26). Eight perils, and his own nation is named second — before the heathen, before the sea, before false brethren. And of the Thessalonians: “For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judaea are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews” (1Th 2:14). A Gentile church suffering from Gentile neighbours is told that it is walking the same road as the Jewish churches of Judaea suffering from their own. The pattern is constant: the sharpest opposition comes from those nearest. The Lord Jesus said it of Himself — “A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house” (Mar 6:4) — and Paul, who was hunted by his own nation, could still write, “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom 9:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a countryman as one born in the same country with another; also an inhabitant of the rural parts, a husbandman.

expand to see more

COUNTRYMAN, n. An inhabitant or native of a region.

2. One born in the same country with another; as, we met a countryman in a foreign land.

3. A rustic; a husbandman; a farmer.

In perils by mine own countrymen. 2 Cor. xi.

Key Scripture

2Co 11:26 — "In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;"

1Th 2:14 — "For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judaea are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews:"

Mar 6:4 — "But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house."

Rom 9:3 — "For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:"

Modern Corruption

Love of one's own nation is either abolished as a prejudice or made an idol, while Paul both suffered from his countrymen and would have been accursed for them.

expand to see more

Romans 9:3 is one of the most extraordinary sentences a converted man ever wrote. Paul's countrymen had stoned him, lain in wait for him, and pursued him from city to city, and he says he could wish himself accursed from Christ for their sake. Two modern positions are equally unable to produce that sentence. The first treats natural affection for one's own people as a prejudice to be repented of, so that love of country becomes suspect in itself; Scripture will not have it, for God set the bounds of the nations, the fifth commandment reaches out to fathers and fatherland, and Christ wept over one particular city. The second position makes the nation the highest good, so that the church becomes a chaplaincy to it and the gospel is measured by what it does for the country. Paul's grief is deep precisely because he does not confuse the two: his kinsmen according to the flesh are dear to him, and their need is not political but Christ.

The catalogue in 2 Corinthians should also be allowed to correct a sentimentality about the church. Paul lists perils among false brethren in the same breath as robbers and shipwreck, and Thessalonica's persecution came from neighbours. The danger to a believer has never been chiefly from strangers; it is from those close enough to have a claim on him. That is why the Lord's word about a prophet in his own country is set in the middle of a passage about His own townsmen, who knew His mother and His brethren and were offended at Him. A Christian who finds his sharpest opposition at home, at work, or among his own people has not fallen out of the ordinary way; he has entered it, and he is in company that includes his Master.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek genos (G1085), race, kindred, nation, at 2 Corinthians 11:26; sumphuletes (G4853), a fellow tribesman, at 1 Thessalonians 2:14; sungenes (G4773), kinsman, at Romans 9:3.

expand to see more

Greek genos (G1085) — race, stock, nation; perils by mine own countrymen; 2 Corinthians 11:26.

Greek sumphuletes (G4853) — a fellow tribesman; ye suffered like things of your own countrymen; 1 Thessalonians 2:14.

Greek sungenes (G4773) — kinsman, of the same family or race; my kinsmen according to the flesh; Romans 9:3.

Greek patris (G3968) — fatherland, one's own country or town; a prophet is not without honour but in his own country; Mark 6:4.

Greek kindunos (G2794) — peril, danger; the word repeated eight times in one verse; 2 Corinthians 11:26.

Usage

"“In perils by mine own countrymen” — named before the heathen and the sea."

"“Ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen” — the pattern is nearness."

"“I could wish that myself were accursed… for my kinsmen according to the flesh” — written by the man they hunted."
